g.text: uint32 — checksum of everything after it

div.p: crc32 — power loss mid-append leaves a partial record. Length-only means you read garbage as valid data. With a checksum, recovery reads until CRC fails and truncates there. A torn tail is expected, not an error.
version — a format without a version byte can never be migrated. Free now, impossible to retrofit.
type — deletes are coming; leaving room costs nothing.
seq — tells you where the snapshot ends and the replay tail begins.
The graph is derived state, never the source of truth. It can always be reconstructed from snapshot + WAL. That is what lets recovery be simple and what makes the write ordering non-negotiable.

g.text: The decision hiding in the snapshot

div.p: Segments at or below the snapshot's seq are deletable — their contents are already captured in snap-000016.bin.

g.text: Recovery — the only time the WAL is read

div.h3: Test this by actually killing the process
div.p: A recovery path verified only by unit tests that call Close() cleanly is a recovery path that has never been tested. Spawn a child, SIGKILL it mid-write, reopen, assert the surviving prefix is exactly consistent.
This is the single highest-value test in the WAL package.

div.h3: Vectors only, or vectors + graph structure?
div.p: Vectors only — small, simple format, but recovery re-inserts everything. Rebuilding 1M × 768 is minutes, not seconds.
Vectors + neighbor lists — larger and fiddlier, but recovery is deserialization.
Start with vectors-only. Then measure recovery time before calling it done. If it is unacceptable, serialize the graph. Do not discover this in production.

g.text: 2 · Load it — rebuild vectors (and graph, if serialized)
3 · Replay WAL records with seq > N
4 · CRC fails on the tail record?

div.p: Deletes. Graph.Delete tombstones a slot: it keeps its index and its edges, so searches still route through it while it is filtered out of results. The operation set the record format has to cover is therefore settled — INSERT and DELETE, with DELETE idempotent so replaying a record twice is safe.
Concurrency. Scratch moved into a pooled searchState and the graph is guarded by an RWMutex, so a WAL writer and readers can coexist without giving up the 2-allocs/op search.
Still open: compaction. Tombstones never release memory on their own, and a rebuild changes every slot index — so a checkpoint written before one cannot be replayed onto a graph compacted after it.

div.p: A torn final record is the normal outcome of a power loss, not corruption. Do not fail the whole recovery for it.
